A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same agent-oriented planning framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across renaming and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy, token-cost and execution-time results, component ablations, and scorer/reward-model experiments in Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original benchmark, transfer, agent-configuration and planning-quality results in Appendices D–F.

M1.justification: The core planner, reward-model architecture and representative-work mechanism remain. v2 extends the detector to identify missing dependencies, retrieve needed prior outputs and trigger additional subtasks (Section 4.4, Appendix F.3 and Figure 15). Appendix B also outlines availability checks and reassignment when agents become unavailable.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only the numerical-reasoning dataset subsequently named Husky-QA; this naming is not new coverage. v2 additionally evaluates decontextualized subsets of DROP and IIRC and complex mathematical problems from MATH, substantially broadening the evaluated data and tasks.

E2.justification: The seven original baselines remain in Table 1 and are reused on DROP/IIRC. The added MATH comparison in Table 5 introduces standalone GPT-3.5, Qwen2-Math-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B alongside GPT-4o, providing a localized expansion of the comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 adds reward-model transfer across datasets, specialized math/code backbones, a configuration with four math agents operating in parallel, and binary LLM assessments of the three planning principles. Appendix C also changes the stated high-score cutoff from 7 to 5, retaining the low cutoff of 1. Original Husky-QA split sizes and reward-model training settings remain; rerunning the retained experiments is not established.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and scorer experiments, v2 adds reward-model generalization tests, expert-agent investigations, direct evaluation of the planning principles, comparisons of agent representations and description sources, and a missing-dependency detector experiment (Appendices D.2, E and F.1–F.3). These substantially expand the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, error bars, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The averaged binary scores introduced in Table 6 are evaluation metrics, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 remain numerically unchanged, including 43.7% main accuracy. New results include 34.0%/41.5% on DROP/IIRC, or 32.0%/39.0% with the transferred reward model; 72% on MATH versus 66% for the best listed individual model; and the principle/description comparisons in Tables 6–8. Appendix F.3 reports 46.2% with dependency checking versus 43.7% without it. These are additional results and conditions, not an unchanged-setting improvement between versions.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(5), the squared-error objective, cosine-based similarity and underlying planning definitions are retained. Notation corrections and explanatory refinements introduce no substantive mathematical revision or new proof.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a planning framework organized around solvability, completeness and non-redundancy, with reward-guided refinement and feedback outperforming single-agent and multi-agent baselines. Naming the framework AOP and adding supporting experiments do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of reward-model transfer, complementary agent representations and description quality. It distinguishes unnecessary subtask redundancy from useful agent redundancy, discusses fault tolerance, and identifies context-window and long-context limitations when scaling agent pools, proposing grouped selection as an extension (Appendices B, D–F). These substantially broaden the applicability and limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 states that code is available and supplies a repository address. v2 also provides the dependency-detection prompt, identifies backbones for added agent configurations, and clarifies that token totals cover the whole test dataset. Existing core prompts, hardware and reward-model training details largely remain.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion is substantially refocused toward multi-agent planning, adding traditional symbolic/RL planning and MA-PDDL, plus newer agent-system references. Broad coverage of reasoning search and external planners, including Tree/Graph of Thoughts and LLM+P, is removed. Publication updates to retained works are distinct from these substantive positioning changes.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 5 to Section 2 and is substantially rewritten. Agent and evaluation prompts are consolidated into Appendix A, reorganizing the supplement. The framework is consistently named AOP, prose is edited throughout, and title, affiliation and contact information are revised.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn and receives an explanatory caption. v2 adds five result tables (Tables 4–8) and the dependency-detection prompt figure, while relocating existing prompt figures and reflowing the document. The original result tables and illustrative Figure 1 are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's single-dataset empirical foundation through additional benchmarks, reward-model transfer tests and direct evaluation of the proposed planning principles. Representation analyses, the dependency-check prompt and explicit scaling limitations also improve scientific understanding and documentation. Added benchmark protocols remain underspecified, and the threshold change is not reconciled with the unchanged original tables, but the broader and more diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.
